problem: Existing robot simulators either have accurate dynamics but poor visuals (Gazebo, MuJoCo, PyBullet) or photorealistic rendering with kinematic-only physics (Habitat, OmniGibson, RoboCasa). None supports full-size humanoid whole-body dynamics together with vision-language perception, and none is designed for education or competitions.
motivation: Full-size humanoid hardware is costly and hard to maintain, so simulation is needed for education and research. Humanoid loco-manipulation and foundation-model integration require both dynamic fidelity and photo-realistic perception. The authors validate the testbed in a nationwide collegiate competition to see where students struggle.
key_idea: Build a humanoid testbed on Isaac Sim (PhysX 5) that co-simulates torque-controlled whole-body dynamics with ray-traced rendering, and ships built-in controllers and a vision-language-action API, then test it in a 137-team competition.
insight: The competition showed that students do well on locomotion with provided controllers (27.55 of 60 points) but poorly on manipulation (<30%) and perception (<20%). Only 11.76% completed Task 6 (vision-language search and transport), and nearly 70% scored zero on the dynamic jumping Task 3. The main lesson is that future humanoid education must emphasize integrating locomotion, manipulation and perception. Compute is also a trilemma: rendering quality, physics time-step and GPU availability trade off, and over 20 launch issues came from missing GPUs.
method: Task module: imports open-source USD assets to build interactive indoor and outdoor scenes with ray-traced lighting, providing egocentric RGB and depth plus contact sensors.
Physics simulation: Isaac Sim Articulations/Robot API with PhysX 5, offering position, velocity and torque joint control (spring-damper for position and velocity modes) and rigid-body collisions.

Robot controllers: built-in Drake-based walking, jumping (centroidal dynamics model) and ZMP step-walking controllers, connected over TCP/IP. The arm controller and high-level planners are left to users.

Action/observation API: joint commands with stiffness and damping, symbolic pick/release (fixed joint created if the end-effector is within 0.2 m of the object or inside an enlarged volume), and observations of joint and body states, cam RGB-D, and language_instruction.
VLA interface: APIs for LLM/VLM integration; Task 6 gives a language instruction plus RGB-D so users can do detection, navigation, pick and place.

Competition design: six independent tasks with a rubric (uneven terrain, valve turning, jumping over a moving bar, slope, steps plus button, indoor object search and transport) on the KUAVO 1.2 m, 34.5 kg, 18-DoF humanoid.
Resource knobs: adjustable rendering resolution and physics time-step, benchmarked on an RTX 4090 with a 0.001 s time-step.

setting.backbone: none (testbed paper; participants build their own planners; built-in Drake model-based controllers)
setting.training_data: none (testbed and competition; no learned model is proposed)
setting.observation: egocentric RGB + depth, joint states, body states (pose and velocity), pick flag, language instruction
setting.action_space: joint position/velocity/torque commands for a 18-DoF humanoid (legs torque-controlled, arms position-controlled) plus symbolic pick/release
setting.privileged: task priors given to users (goal center position, valve position, object 3D models, slope angle, bar state); no privileged data beyond these

numbers_note: No navigation benchmark results; only competition statistics (percent of teams per score) and FPS vs resolution. Only 51 valid submissions from 137 teams.
results: 137 teams (402 participants) joined and 51 valid submissions were received. Full-mark rates were 52.94% (Task 1), 19.61% (Task 2), 50.98% (Task 4), 37.25% (Task 5), and 11.76% (Task 6), and nearly 70% scored zero on Task 3. In the later physical competition, the top 10 teams averaged 75%, 80%, 63% and 83% on valve turning, button pressing, uneven walking and door opening, but only 5% on the indoor object search task.
limitations: Manipulation is simplified (fixed-joint pick when close, no dexterous grasping), and fine-grained grasping is left to future work.
There is a sim-to-real gap in damping, friction and lighting.

It requires an NVIDIA GPU, and frame rates are modest (about 14-17 FPS on an RTX 4090). No quantitative navigation or VLA benchmark is reported, and the scene diversity is small (three objects, one apartment).
